### Objective W11-15 — Therapeutic index {#w11-lo15}

**Original objective:** How do you calculate a therapeutic index of a drug

Give the ratio, calculate TI for TD50 = 400 units and ED50 = 20 units, and interpret its limits.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Use **TI = TD50/ED50**, or LD50/ED50 when lethality is the endpoint. Here **400/20 = 20** (unitless, using comparable dose units). A larger ratio indicates greater separation between the effective and toxic median doses under those test conditions. It does not guarantee safety for every individual. The lecture diagram labels ED50, although nearby text also uses EC50; this exercise explicitly supplies doses and uses ED50.

**Source:** Week 11 objectives, item 15; Lecture 11, PDF p. 23; Tutorial 7, PDF p. 4.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-lo15 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Calculate 400/20 = 20 with toxic dose above effective dose and matching units that cancel. The result compares the supplied median dose endpoints. It cannot establish that every individual has the same response or convert the ratio into a safe personal dose.

Write the formula before inserting values: **TI = TD50/ED50**. With TD50 = 400 units and ED50 = 20 units, **TI = 400/20 = 20**. Matching dose units cancel, leaving a dimensionless ratio. Reversing the fraction would give 0.05 and would not be the index defined in this exercise.

The result means the toxic median dose is twenty times the effective median dose under the specified test conditions. It does not mean a recommended dose of twenty units, a twenty-hour half-life, or guaranteed safety for everyone below a particular value. When the measured adverse endpoint is lethality, the lecture uses LD50 in the numerator instead.

The question deliberately supplies doses and uses ED50. The documented ED50/EC50 wording issue in the lecture should not be resolved by silently replacing a dose ratio with a concentration ratio. Keep the calculation and interpretation aligned with the values actually provided.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
:::

### Objective W11-16 — Agonist and antagonist {#w11-lo16}

**Original objective:** What is an agonist and an antagonist

Define BOTH terms and explain why binding alone does not demonstrate receptor activation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
An agonist binds a receptor and elicits a response. An antagonist binds without activating that response and blocks or reduces the agonist's action. Both can bind the receptor; the difference is what binding does to signaling, not whether binding occurs at all.

**Source:** Week 11 objectives, item 16; Lecture 11, agonist/antagonist slides; Tutorial 7.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-lo16 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
A receptor can be occupied without being activated. That is why the agonist–antagonist distinction depends on the signaling consequence of binding, not just the presence of binding. An antagonist reduces the effect of an activating ligand without eliciting that response itself.

Receptor occupancy and receptor activation are separate observations. An agonist binds and produces the relevant receptor-mediated response. An antagonist also binds, but does not activate that response and reduces or blocks the action of an agonist. Thus the difference is not whether the molecule can recognize the receptor at all.

This matters when interpreting a binding experiment. Showing that a ligand occupies a receptor does not establish that the downstream signal turns on; a functional measurement is needed to distinguish activation from blockade in this course model. Similarly, a ligand that prevents an activating ligand's effect should not be called an agonist simply because it binds strongly. Keep this receptor terminology separate from the preceding enzyme-inhibition examples, where the target and mechanism were COX/PGHS substrate access rather than receptor activation.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
:::

# Part C — Integrated Practice

### Integrated Question 1 — Platelet prediction
A platelet is exposed briefly to aspirin and then washed free of drug. Predict TxA2 production over the following hours.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
TxA2 production remains strongly reduced because aspirin covalently inhibited the platelet COX enzyme, and the anucleate platelet cannot readily replace it by new transcription and protein synthesis.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-ix01 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Washing removes unbound drug but does not reverse the covalent modification already made to platelet COX. The course model emphasizes that the platelet cannot readily replace the inhibited enzyme. Continued suppression of TxA2 therefore follows even after the brief exposure ends.

The wash removes free aspirin, but the experiment has already exposed COX to a covalent modifying agent. That modification is not undone merely by removing drug from the solution. Platelet COX activity therefore remains reduced in the course model, lowering PGH2 production and consequently the TxA2 made by platelet thromboxane synthase.

The platelet context explains why the inhibition persists over the subsequent observation. Platelets are anucleate and cannot readily replace the inhibited enzyme through the replacement process emphasized in the lecture. By contrast, a reversible inhibitor need not leave the same persistent enzyme lesion after removal. The prediction is therefore continued strong suppression of TxA2, not an immediate return to the untreated level simply because the surrounding drug has been washed away. The question does not specify enough information for a precise recovery curve; its purpose is to connect covalent binding, limited enzyme replacement, and persistent pathway inhibition.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 2 — COX-2 inhibitor
A drug is too bulky to fit the narrower COX-1 substrate channel but fits COX-2. What is the intended pharmacological consequence?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Preferential COX-2 inhibition should reduce inflammatory prostaglandin production while preserving more COX-1 housekeeping activity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-ix02 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The stated size difference gives the inhibitor a structural preference for COX-2. Preferential inhibition can suppress more inflammatory activity while leaving more COX-1 housekeeping activity intact. That intended selectivity is not a claim that the drug is risk-free.

Translate the structural observation into a target preference. The drug fits the larger COX-2 channel but is excluded from the narrower COX-1 channel, so it is intended to inhibit COX-2 preferentially. Less COX-2 activity means less contribution to the inflammatory prostaglandin pathway described by the course, while relatively preserved COX-1 can maintain more of its housekeeping contribution.

That reasoning supports an intended selective effect, not a universal guarantee about every tissue response or adverse outcome. The source explicitly distinguishes selectivity from being risk-free. It would also be incorrect to say the drug activates COX-1, blocks all eicosanoid synthesis permanently, or inhibits PLA2 merely because it is part of the same broader pathway. The key sequence is channel size, molecular fit, preferential enzyme inhibition, and the corresponding functional aim. No treatment recommendation or dosage follows from the hypothetical structural comparison.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 3 — TI calculation
Drug A has an ED50 of 5 mg and TD50 of 500 mg. Calculate its therapeutic index.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$TI=500/5=100$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-ix03 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
Use the supplied doses in the stated order: TD50/ED50 = 500 mg/5 mg. The result is 100 and the mg units cancel. Inverting the values would describe the reciprocal ratio rather than the therapeutic index requested.

Use the supplied toxic and effective doses in the defined order: **TI = TD50/ED50 = 500 mg / 5 mg = 100**. The milligram units cancel because the same dose unit appears in numerator and denominator. The answer is therefore 100, not 100 mg. Subtracting would give a dose difference rather than the requested index, and reversing the ratio would give 0.01.

Interpret the ratio as a hundred-fold separation between the two measured median-dose endpoints under the stated test conditions. It does not identify a recommended dose, describe how long the drug stays in circulation, or guarantee that every individual is unaffected below 500 mg. Those would require information beyond this exercise. A complete solution includes the formula, substitution, unit cancellation, numerical result, and the limited meaning of that result, rather than only writing the final number.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
:::

### Integrated Question 4 — Metabolism and bioavailability
A second drug strongly inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzyme that normally metabolizes Drug X. What may happen to Drug X bioavailability?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Drug X may remain in circulation longer and at higher concentration because its metabolic clearance is slowed. Its bioavailability and effective exposure may therefore increase.
:::

::: {.callout-note .question-explanation #explanation-w11-ix04 collapse="true" title="Explanation"}
The question specifies inhibition of the enzyme that normally clears Drug X through metabolism. Slower metabolism can therefore prolong its presence in circulation and increase exposure in the lecture's operational sense. This prediction follows from the stated clearance pathway, not from assuming all drug interactions act identically.

The hypothetical specifies that the inhibited P450 enzyme normally metabolizes Drug X. Reducing that metabolic route can slow removal of the original drug from circulation. With less efficient metabolic clearance, Drug X may persist longer and reach a higher circulating concentration than it otherwise would under comparable exposure conditions.

The question uses bioavailability in the lecture's operational sense of circulating amount available to reach the target, so the answer describes increased or prolonged exposure in that sense. The word may should be retained: no dose schedule, quantitative clearance rate, or contribution of other elimination routes is provided, so an exact concentration or half-life change cannot be calculated. Do not infer that the drug necessarily becomes more therapeutically useful or that every P450 interaction has the same consequence. The supported prediction is conditional on the stated role of this enzyme in metabolizing Drug X.

**Review:** [Week 11 study guide](../study-guides/week11-lipids-eicosanoids-drugs.qmd).
